Option A: Panic disorder Option B: Agoraphobia Option C: Adverse reaction to ramipril Option D: Generalised anxiety disorder Option E: Phaeochromocytoma The correct answer is Option E.

### Response:
chosen: Panic disorder - characterised by recurrent unexpected panic attacks that are accompanied by at least 1 physical symptom. Agoraphobia - develop anxiety when they find themselves in places or situations where they perceive they might not be able to escape if they feel an attack coming on. Adverse reaction to ramipril - although this patients reported that he'd suffered palpitations since being put on ramipril (which is known to have side effects including hypotension and bradycardia [therefore making  tachycardia more likely in other patients]), however overall his pulse rate still seems quite high and so if this was caused solely by the ramipril it is likely to be due to an adverse drug reaction rather than disease. Note that if the patient had previously been suffering with excessively rapid heart rates even before starting taking the ramipril then it would be much more likely that the ramipril is inducing the elevated heart rates. Generalised anxiety disorder - main feature is persistent and chronic anxiety which often occurs in association with (but is not usually as severe as) identifiable stressors, and without concurrent symptoms of psychosis.Phaeochromocytoma - rare tumour (normally benign) of the medulla of the adrenal gland, associated with over-production of adrenaline and therefore resulting in hypertension (with corresponding tachycardia). Key features suggesting this diagnoses include: - Patients reports that he is hypertensive despite previous treatment and is now complaining of his blood pressure again
rejected: The fact that this patient is experiencing palpitations with a high heart rate and is on anti-hypertensive medication suggests that this patient may have hyperadrenalism. This can be caused by pheochromocytoma or adrenal adenomas. Patients with these conditions can experience episodes of severe hypertension which can lead to symptoms such as headache, palpitation, tachycardia and hyperventilation. Weight loss and intense feelings of panic have also been reported in some patients. These symptoms usually come in episodes which can last for a few days up to a few months. Between these episodes patients are usually asymptomatic. As this patient is presenting with symptoms indicative of hyperadrenalism coupled with palpitations and a high heart rate, the most likely diagnosis is phaeochromocytoma (also known as adrenal pheochromocytoma). This is a neuroendocrine tumour arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal glands. It accounts for less than 0.1% of all cases of cancer. This condition is rare however it’s important to recognise it because it can be fatal if it goes untreated. Patients who suffer from this condition should be managed in specialised centres. Treatment options include pharmacological treatment, surgical resection and radiotherapy.

### Response:
chosen: The correct answer should be D) local vasoconstriction This is because when there is a low V/Q ratio this means that the alveoli are being poorly ventilated but are still receiving normal perfusion. Therefore the alveoli are becoming hypoventilated which then leads to a rise in pCO2 and a fall in pO2 (the alveolar gas exchange).  Therefore the body will sense a rise in pCO2 leading to an increase in respiratory rate as part of a regulatory mechanism. However despite an increase in RR, the alveolar-arterial gradient will still remain high. Therefore it is better to match regional ventilation and blood flow in order to improve gas exchange efficiency. As there is poor matching between regional ventilation and blood flow, one way to improve the V/Q ratio is by altering the regional blood flow. Blood flow can be altered via the use of smooth muscle tone within the walls of the blood vessels. The primary control mechanism for the diameter of blood vessels is the intrinsic tone of the vascular smooth muscle itself. ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) is released from cardiomyocytes in the atria in response to raised blood volume or pressure. rejected: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria (HGPS) is caused by a mutation in LMNA gene. This mutation causes alternative splicing of LMNA pre-mRNA resulting in the loss of exons 11 and 12.
